expectations.text: Applies at least five named models
expectations.evidence: Sections 1-9 apply all nine Vol. 1 models by their correct names (Map Is Not the Territory, Circle of Competence, First Principles, Thought Experiment, Second-Order, Probabilistic, Inversion, Occam's, Hanlon's), each with book tools matching SKILL.md (e.g. the three map tools, Lifer/Stranger, LeBron vs Woody Allen/Durant).

expectations.text: Uses second-order thinking with concrete consequences
expectations.evidence: Section 5: 'your income now has to come from furniture. You start taking deals you'd have passed on... Healthcare costs show up. Seasonal dips hit your rent'; 10-year 'gap on your résumé and less retirement saved'. Cobra bounty example matches SKILL.md. The 10/10/10 framing is SKILL.md's '(std framing)' and is not credited to the book.

expectations.text: Uses inversion (e.g. what would guarantee failure)
expectations.evidence: Section 7: 'How would I guarantee this fails?' with 8 failure conditions ('Quit with less than 3 months of savings', 'Skip health insurance'), then 'do the opposite'. Jacobi quote and Lewin's 5-step force field analysis match SKILL.md.

expectations.text: Uses circle of competence and/or probabilistic thinking with numbers
expectations.evidence: Circle of competence: Lifer vs Stranger, curiosity/monitoring/feedback, and the three outside-the-circle steps all match SKILL.md. Probabilistic section has numbers: 'cut your projected revenue by 20-30% and add 20-30% to your costs', and the book's '20-40% returns' asymmetry example. Small embellishment: 'The book warns that we remember wins and forget losses' is not in SKILL.md, but it fits the monitoring idea and does not drive the assertion.

expectations.text: Ends with a decision rule or test, not just a list
expectations.evidence: Ends with 'a falsifiable go/no-go rule: 3 months in a row of profit >= 60-70% of my take-home pay' and the fallback 'If by month 9 I'm below $___, I start applying for jobs'.

expectations.text: Defines Occam's razor correctly
expectations.evidence: 'Simpler explanations are more likely to be true. Prefer the one with the fewest moving parts.' This matches SKILL.md exactly.

expectations.text: Defines Hanlon's razor correctly
expectations.evidence: 'Don't put down to malice what is more easily explained by stupidity. The likeliest explanation has the least intent.' This matches SKILL.md. The road-rage example and 'the Devil Fallacy' are correctly cited.

expectations.text: Applies both to the ghosting scenario
expectations.evidence: Part 2 lists 7 explanations, scores them by assumptions under Occam (Step 2) and by intent under Hanlon (Step 3), and shows where the razors diverge (Step 4: '#4 is fairly simple, so Occam alone doesn't rule it out. It's Hanlon that pushes it down').

expectations.text: Uses first principles (breaking down to fundamentals, Socratic questioning or Five Whys) on pricing
expectations.evidence: Part 3 breaks price into irreducible parts (cost floor, time, holding cost, buyer value ceiling, demand). It applies the book's six Socratic steps, matching SKILL.md ('consider other views' ~ 'consider alternatives'), runs a Five Whys chain ending in 'Root cause: presentation, not price', and rebuilds a $375 price.

expectations.text: Notes limits of the razors
expectations.evidence: Table caveats: Occam 'Some things really aren't simple' (matches SKILL.md's caveat and medical sidebar); Hanlon 'Malice does exist. The razor sets your default'. Closing caveat: 'some people really are acting in bad faith'. Note: the claim that the book's Occam example is 'Medicine: the common cause of a symptom is more likely than a rare one' goes beyond SKILL.md, which only names a 'medical-field sidebar', but it does not contradict it.

expectations.text: Applies at least five named models
expectations.evidence: Lists all nine Vol. 1 models correctly and applies seven in depth (sections 1-7), plus the razors briefly in '8 & 9'. The names match SKILL.md.

expectations.text: Uses second-order thinking with concrete consequences
expectations.evidence: Section 5 table: 'Lose employer health insurance and 401(k) match... Harder to get a mortgage (lenders often want 2 years of self-employment history)', 'push local prices down by flooding your own market', 'career skills and network fade'.

expectations.text: Uses inversion (e.g. what would guarantee failure)
expectations.evidence: Section 7 'How to make sure this fails': 8 items ('Quit with less than 3 months of savings', 'Depend 100% on one platform'), each turned into a rule. This is generic; it has no Jacobi or force field, but it is correct inversion.

expectations.text: Uses circle of competence and/or probabilistic thinking with numbers
expectations.evidence: Probabilistic section with numbers: 'Bad case (say 30%)... Base case (say 50%)... Good case (say 20%)', plus fat tails and base rates. Circle of competence is applied correctly but generically (no Lifer/Stranger or the book's three steps).

expectations.text: Ends with a decision rule or test, not just a list
expectations.evidence: 'Putting It Together: A Decision Rule' - 'Quit when all of these are true' with 6 testable conditions (e.g. 3-6 months net profit >= 60-75% of take-home, 6-12 months runway) and a written exit ramp. The 'one-way/two-way door' framing is not presented as the book's.

expectations.text: Defines Occam's razor correctly
expectations.evidence: 'When several explanations fit the facts, prefer the simplest one, the one that needs the fewest assumptions.' This is correct and consistent with SKILL.md.

expectations.text: Defines Hanlon's razor correctly
expectations.evidence: 'Never attribute to malice that which is adequately explained by stupidity... It's about intent'. This is correct and consistent with SKILL.md (no book examples given).

expectations.text: Applies both to the ghosting scenario
expectations.evidence: Lists 6 stories, then 'Apply Occam's Razor' (stories 1-3 need 'a motive, a plan, and a reason to target you') and 'Apply Hanlon's Razor' (story 3 is a malice story), each with its own verdict and actions.

expectations.text: Uses first principles (breaking down to fundamentals, Socratic questioning or Five Whys) on pricing
expectations.evidence: 'breaking a problem down to its basic truths and building up from there, instead of copying'. Steps 1-7 derive what a price must do, list every cost ($135), price the hours (10h x $25), find the buyer ceiling, and compare floor vs ceiling. This is genuine decomposition; it has no Socratic questioning or Five Whys, but the assertion allows any of them.

expectations.text: Notes limits of the razors
expectations.evidence: 'Both razors are rules of thumb, not laws... At that point the simplest explanation really is fraud. The razors help you default to the likely answer. They don't tell you to ignore evidence.'
